title: Designing an experiment
objectives: Use randomisation, blocking and replication to design an experiment.

screens.title: Who chose the algorithm
screens.prose: A trader lets each portfolio manager pick algorithm X or Y for their order. Y's average shortfall is 11.5 bps, X's only 3.0. The table shows eight of the orders.
screens.question: What is the problem with concluding that X is better?

options.text: Every volatile name went to Y, so volatility and algorithm are tangled

options.why: More orders chosen the same way would keep the same tangle. Size does not fix how the orders were assigned.

options.text: Nothing: Y's shortfall is much larger
options.why: Volatile names cost more to trade whatever the algorithm. Y got all of them.

options.text: Shortfall should be in pounds, not bps
options.why: Bps are the usual unit; the trouble is who chose.

hints.text: Look at the volatility column beside the algorithm column.
All three high-volatility orders went to Y.
The managers' choice is confounded with volatility.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the volatility of the orders each algorithm got.

byKey.none: You read the gap as the algorithm's effect. The managers sent the hard orders to Y.

explain.text: Y received every volatile order, and volatile orders cost more to trade. The cure is **randomisation**: a coin, not a person, picks the algorithm, so volatility cannot follow the choice.

screens.title: A coin within each stock-day
screens.prose: Each stock-day has a morning and an afternoon order. Alternating, A every morning, would tangle the algorithm with time of day. Instead a coin decides per stock-day: heads sends the morning order to A. The coins came up H, T, T, H for VOD, BP, HSBA, AZN.
screens.question: Put each order in its arm.

hints.text: Heads: morning to A, afternoon to B. Tails: the reverse.
VOD heads, BP tails, HSBA tails, AZN heads.
A gets VOD am, BP pm, HSBA pm and AZN am.

feedback.correct: Each stock-day has one order in each arm, and the coin decided which.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply each stock's coin to its two orders.

byKey.vod-am: VOD came up heads, so its morning order goes to A.
byKey.bp-am: BP came up tails, so its morning order goes to B.
byKey.hsba-am: HSBA came up tails: morning to B.
byKey.azn-am: AZN came up heads: morning to A.

explain.text: Every stock-day sends one order to each arm, so stock and day cancel in the comparison. The coin makes time of day equally likely to favour either arm.

screens.title: How many orders
screens.prose:
To detect $\delta = 1$ bp when shortfall has $\sigma = 8$ bps, at 5% two-sided with 80% power, each arm needs
$$n = \frac{2(z_{0.975} + z_{0.8})^2\sigma^2}{\delta^2}, \quad z_{0.975} = 1.95996, \; z_{0.8} = 0.84162$$
Slide $n$ and watch the hatched power under the dashed curve, the statistic when the effect is real.
screens.question: How many orders per arm, rounded up?

hints.text: Add the two quantiles first.

feedback.correct: 1,005 per arm; statsmodels' `NormalIndPower` agrees, and the $t$ version asks 1,006.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Square the sum of the quantiles, then multiply by $2\sigma^2/\delta^2 = 128$.

byKey.half: You left out the factor 2. Both arms' means are estimated, so the difference has variance $2\sigma^2/n$.
byKey.sd: You used $\sigma = 8$ instead of $\sigma^2 = 64$, or a similar slip.

explain.text: $n = 2 \times 7.849 \times 64 = 1{,}004.66$, so 1,005 per arm. At that $n$ the alternative sits 2.80 standard errors out and 80% of it lies past 1.96.

screens.title: A month is not enough
screens.prose: The desk can only run 200 orders per arm in a month. The standard error of the difference is then $8\sqrt{2/200} = 0.8$ bps, so the alternative sits $1/0.8 = 1.25$ standard errors out.
screens.question: What is the power with 200 orders per arm?

hints.text: Read the hatched area at $n = 200$.

feedback.correct: 24%: a real 1 bp gain is missed three times in four.

byKey.alpha: 5% is the false-alarm rate, not the power.
byKey.half: 50% would need the alternative at 1.96 standard errors.

explain.text: Power is $P(Z > 0.71) = 24\%$. A month of unblocked orders would usually say no difference even if the new algorithm is 1 bp better.

screens.title: Blocking on the stock-day
screens.prose: Most of an order's shortfall is its stock-day: the two orders in one stock-day correlate at $\rho = 0.8$. Analyse each stock-day's difference $D = Y_B - Y_A$, with $\operatorname{Var}(D) = 2\sigma^2(1 - \rho)$.
screens.question: What is the standard deviation of $D$?

hints.text: Put $\sigma^2 = 64$ and $1 - \rho = 0.2$ into the variance.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the square root of $2 \times 64 \times 0.2$.

byKey.var: That is the variance. Take its square root.
byKey.indep: That ignores the shared stock-day. Pairing removes it.

explain.text: The stock-day's own noise cancels in $D$, leaving $\sqrt{25.6} = 5.06$ bps. That is **blocking**: compare treatments inside units that share their noise.

screens.title: Pairs needed
screens.prose: With pairs, $n = (z_{0.975} + z_{0.8})^2\operatorname{SD}(D)^2/\delta^2$ stock-days, each giving one order to each arm.
screens.question: How many stock-days give 80% power for $\delta = 1$ bp?

hints.text: $\operatorname{SD}(D)^2 = 25.6$.

feedback.correct: 201 stock-days, against 1,005 orders per arm unblocked. With 200 pairs power is 79.8%.

byKey.arm: That is the unblocked count. Pairing cuts the variance by $1 - \rho = 0.2$.
byKey.twice: You kept the factor 2. It is already inside $\operatorname{SD}(D)^2 = 2\sigma^2(1 - \rho)$.

explain.text: $n(1 - \rho) = 1{,}005 \times 0.2 \approx 201$ pairs. The month of 200 stock-days now has 79.8% power, if the analysis keeps the pairs.

screens.title: Blocked, then analysed apart
screens.prose: The desk ran 200 stock-day pairs, as designed. An analyst then compares the 200 A orders with the 200 B orders by Welch's two-sample test.
screens.question: What does the two-sample analysis do?

options.text: It leaves the shared stock-day noise in the variance, throwing away the blocking's power
Nothing: the same orders give the same answer
options.why: Same orders, different variance. Welch's test uses $11.31/\sqrt{200}$, not $5.06/\sqrt{200}$.

options.text: It biases the estimate of the difference
options.why: The mean difference is the same; only its standard error is too large.

options.text: It is fine, because randomisation guarantees balance in any one sample
options.why: Randomisation balances on average, not in every sample, and it does not shrink the variance.

hints.text: Which variance does a two-sample test use?
It treats the 400 orders as unrelated.
Its power falls to about 6%: its SE of 0.8 bps is twice the true 0.36.

feedback.correct: The analysis must follow the design.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the standard error each analysis uses.

byKey.same: You assumed the analysis does not matter. Ignoring the pairs puts the stock-day noise back.
byKey.balance: You leaned on randomisation. It removes bias, not variance.

explain.text: Analysed apart, the test uses a standard error of 0.8 bps, but the estimate varies by only 0.36. Its power falls to about 6%, below even the 24% of unpaired orders. Lesson 9 shows it on real numbers: $p = 0.22$ unpaired against 0.006 paired.

screens.title: Where the sample-size formula comes from
screens.prose: Derive $n$ for a two-sided 5% test with 80% power. One line forgets the power: leave it out.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: $\bar D = \bar Y_B - \bar Y_A$ has standard error $\text{SE} = \sigma\sqrt{2/n}$, from two independent means
Under no effect, reject when $\bar D > z_{0.975}\,\text{SE}$, the upper cut of the 5% test
Under the effect $\bar D \sim N(\delta, \text{SE}^2)$; 80% power needs the cut $z_{0.8}$ SEs below $\delta$
So $\delta = (z_{0.975} + z_{0.8})\,\sigma\sqrt{2/n}$, equating the two positions of the cut
Power needs $\delta = z_{0.975}\,\text{SE}$, putting the effect on the cut
lines.why: With the effect exactly on the cut, half the alternative lies beyond it: 50% power, not 80%.

hints.text: Start with the standard error of the difference.
Place the cut under the null, then under the effect.
The cut sits $z_{0.975}$ SEs above 0 and $z_{0.8}$ SEs below $\delta$.

feedback.correct: Two quantiles add because the cut must be far from both means.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. SE, the cut under the null, the cut under the effect, then solve.

byKey.x: You put the effect on the cut. That gives 50% power.

explain.text: The cut is $z_{0.975}$ SEs above 0 and $z_{0.8}$ SEs below $\delta$, so $\delta$ spans both. Halving $\delta$ quadruples $n$.

screens.title: Size and randomise in code
screens.prose: Write the two tools a design needs. `norm.ppf(0.975)` is $z_{0.975}$. For the assignment, use `np.random.default_rng(seed)` so the same seed gives the same plan.

Group the order indices by block first.

screens.title: Run it for a month and see
screens.prose: The head of trading says: "run the new algorithm for a month and see whether shortfall improves". You expect about 1 bp, shortfall has $\sigma = 8$ bps, and two orders in a stock-day correlate at 0.8.
screens.question: Which reply is a design?

options.text: Unit: one parent order. Block: the stock-day. A coin per stock-day sends one order to each algorithm. Run 201 stock-days and analyse the pairs
Switch to the new algorithm for a month and compare with last month
options.why: Months differ in volatility and flow, so the comparison is confounded with time.

options.text: Send every order to both algorithms
options.why: An order can only be worked once. The pair is two orders in one stock-day.

options.text: Run 1,005 orders per arm, analysed as two samples
options.why: That works but wastes the blocking: 201 pairs give the same power.

hints.text: A design names the unit, the block, the randomisation and the size.
The block is what the two orders share.
201 stock-day pairs, analysed as pairs.

feedback.correct: Unit, block, randomisation and size, with the analysis to match.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Look for the answer that names all four choices.

byKey.month: You proposed a before and after comparison. Time is then confounded with the algorithm.

explain.text: 201 blocked pairs give the power of 1,005 orders per arm. Lesson 9 runs this experiment and analyses it.

ideas: Randomise so nothing about an order can follow the algorithm; letting people choose confounds the comparison.
Replicate enough: $n = 2(z_{0.975} + z_{0.8})^2\sigma^2/\delta^2$, 1,005 orders per arm for 1 bp at $\sigma = 8$.
Block on what orders share: with $\rho = 0.8$ in a stock-day, 201 pairs give the same power. The analysis must keep the pairs.

formula.name: Sample size
formula.note: $\rho = 0$ for independent arms; with blocking $n$ counts pairs.

summary.trap: Blocking the design and then analysing two independent samples throws the power gain away.

quiz.prose: In a paired execution test, one stock-day had only its A order because the B order was cancelled.
quiz.question: What does that stock-day add to the paired comparison?

options.text: Nothing: with no B order it has no difference to contribute

options.why: A paired comparison uses differences. One order alone has no difference.

options.text: An extra A observation that sharpens the estimate
options.why: In the paired analysis it is dropped; adding it to the A mean would reintroduce the stock-day noise.

feedback.correct: A block with one order contributes nothing.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The analysis works on within-block differences.

explain.text: Each block contributes one difference $D = Y_B - Y_A$. Without a B order there is no difference, so the block drops out.

quiz.prose: A test needs 1,005 orders per arm to detect 1 bp.
quiz.question: About how many per arm does it need to detect 2 bps, all else equal?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. $n$ is proportional to $1/\delta^2$.

byKey.same: A larger effect needs fewer orders.

explain.text: $n \propto 1/\delta^2$, so doubling the effect divides $n$ by 4: $1{,}004.66/4 = 251.2$, so 252.

quiz.prose: A desk randomises 40 orders between two algorithms by coin.
quiz.question: What does randomisation guarantee?

options.text: That no characteristic of the orders can systematically follow the algorithm
That both arms get the same mix of volatile names in this sample
options.why: Balance holds on average. In one sample of 40 the mix can still differ by chance.
Power comes from the sample size and the design, not the coin.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Randomisation removes bias, not chance imbalance.

explain.text: A coin cannot know an order's volatility, so differences between arms are noise, not bias. Blocking removes known noise as well.
